name: Hagia Sophia
desc: The dome floats on forty windows and the light coming through them is the whole point; nothing built for another nine hundred years came close to the span. Since it returned to use as a mosque the ground floor is carpeted and the Deesis mosaic is seen from the upper gallery, reached by a stone ramp worn into grooves.
season: Nov–Mar for the light and the short queues — May and September mean two-hour lines
tip: Foreigners now enter through the north side and go straight up to the gallery; the 09:00 opening buys you twenty quiet minutes before the tour groups reach the ramp.
todo: Deesis mosaic in the south gallery
Marble Door and the empress loge
Viking graffiti scratched on a parapet
rev: Nearly everyone calls the interior overwhelming, then complains that the carpet and the ground-floor screens cut off the great floor, that the audio guide is compulsory in the foreigner ticket, and that the queue outside has no shade.
entry: ≈€25 for foreign visitors, upper gallery route · not covered by the Museum Pass
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M11+M2+T1 tram, or Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then the ferry from Kadıköy to Eminönü and one tram stop

name: Blue Mosque (Sultan Ahmed Mosque)
desc: Six minarets, a cascade of half-domes, and inside more than twenty thousand İznik tiles that read blue-green only in strong light. The courtyard is the better half of the building: a rectangle of grey stone and pigeons with the dome rising behind the arcade. It is a working mosque, closed to visitors five times a day.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the courtyard is a furnace in August afternoons
tip: Go about 30 minutes after the dawn or the late-evening prayer, when the tour groups are absent and the chandeliers are lit low over the carpet.
todo: Enter through the west courtyard gate
Tiles in the upper gallery light
Sultan's pavilion and the carpet detail
rev: Visitors love the courtyard and the free entry, then note that the tourist rope keeps you at the back third of the hall, that the interior is dimmer than the photographs suggest, and that touts on the approach are relentless.
entry: Free · modest dress required, headscarves lent at the door
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M11+M2 and the T1 tram to Sultanahmet; the mosque is a two-minute walk from the stop

name: Topkapı Palace
desc: Not one building but four courtyards that get progressively quieter, ending at a marble terrace looking down on the Bosphorus where the sultans sat. The Harem is a separate warren of tiled rooms and cold corridors. The treasury holds the Topkapı dagger and an eighty-six carat diamond, and the queue for them moves slowly.
season: Apr–May and Oct — closed Tuesdays; July courtyards have almost no shade
tip: Buy the Harem supplement and do the Harem first thing, before the coaches arrive around 10:30 and turn its narrow corridors into a shuffle.
todo: Harem's tiled Twin Kiosk
Baghdad Kiosk terrace over the Bosphorus
Imperial Council chamber and its grilled window
rev: Most agree the terrace views and the Harem justify the day, while complaints centre on the treasury bottleneck, the sharply raised foreigner price, sections shut for restoration without warning, and thin labelling in English.
entry: ≈€45 including the Harem · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye · closed Tuesdays
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then metro and the T1 tram to Gülhane or Sultanahmet; the Gülhane gate is the quieter entrance

name: Hippodrome of Constantinople
desc: A long park where a chariot track used to be, with three survivors standing in a line down the old spine: an Egyptian obelisk of Thutmose III on a carved Byzantine base, the bronze Serpent Column looted from Delphi, and a stripped masonry pillar. The ground level of the track sits several metres below the modern paving.
season: Year-round — best in spring evenings when locals take over the benches
tip: Walk down to the obelisk base and read the relief of Theodosius watching the races; it shows the monument being raised, and almost nobody stops for it.
todo: Theodosius reliefs on the obelisk base
Serpent Column from Delphi
German Fountain's gold mosaic dome
rev: People are often underwhelmed until they read the base reliefs, and complaints run to carpet-shop touts working the square, no shade and no explanatory signage worth the name.
entry: Free
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M11+M2 and the T1 tram to Sultanahmet, which stops at the north end of the square

name: Basilica Cistern
desc: Three hundred and thirty-six columns in shallow water under the street, cool and echoing even in August. Two Medusa heads reused as column bases sit in the far corner, one sideways, one upside down, for reasons nobody has settled. The 2022 restoration added coloured lighting and contemporary sculptures that divide opinion sharply.
season: Year-round — the single reliable cool refuge in July and August
tip: Book the first slot of the day online; from mid-morning the walkways are single file and the reflections are ruined by phone torches.
todo: The two Medusa head bases
Column of the Tears carving
Reflections from the far walkway
rev: Everyone agrees the space is remarkable and cool; complaints are consistent about the new coloured lighting and installed artworks, the queue outside, and a foreigner price that has roughly tripled since 2021.
entry: ≈€25–30 day ticket, night ticket dearer · not covered by the Museum Pass
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then metro and the T1 tram to Sultanahmet; the entrance is 100 m north of Hagia Sophia

name: Süleymaniye Mosque
desc: Sinan's best building in the city, sitting on the third hill with a terrace that drops straight to the Golden Horn. Inside it is plain by Ottoman standards — white walls, red-and-white voussoirs, one band of İznik around the mihrab — and it works better for that. The tombs of Süleyman and Roxelana stand in the garden behind.
season: Year-round; late afternoon in Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct for the terrace light
tip: Come out of the north gate to the terrace wall at sunset, then eat kuru fasulye at one of the bean shops on Şifahane Sokak behind the complex.
todo: Terrace view over the Golden Horn
Tombs of Süleyman and Hürrem
Sinan's own small tomb at the corner
rev: Regularly called more moving than the Blue Mosque and much less crowded; complaints are about the steep cobbled approach, closures at prayer times and student crowds from the university filling the terrace at dusk.
entry: Free
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then metro to Vezneciler (M2) and a 10-min walk uphill, or the T1 tram to Eminönü and a stiff climb

name: Zeyrek Mosque (Pantokrator Monastery)
desc: Three twelfth-century Byzantine churches joined into one brick mass, once the imperial monastery of the Pantokrator and burial place of the Comneni. Restoration finished in 2023 revealed the opus sectile floor of coloured marble under the south church. Around it, the last streets of leaning Ottoman timber houses in Fatih.
season: Year-round — the sloping lanes are slippery in winter rain
tip: Ask the caretaker to lift the protective boarding over the marble floor of the south church; he usually will if you come outside prayer times and ask politely.
todo: Opus sectile floor in the south church
Brickwork from the Golden Horn side
Timber houses on Zeyrek Mehmet Paşa Sokak
rev: Visitors who make the climb call it the best Byzantine building nobody visits, but note the confusing opening hours, the fenced-off north church and a neighbourhood that feels shabby and unsignposted.
entry: Free · working mosque, closed to visitors around prayer times
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M2 metro to Vezneciler and a 15-min walk down through Zeyrek, or the Golden Horn ferry to Unkapanı and a steep climb

name: Theodosian Land Walls
desc: Six and a half kilometres of fifth-century triple fortification from the Sea of Marmara to the Golden Horn: outer wall, inner wall of ninety-six towers, and a moat now planted with market gardens. Sections are restored, sections are rubble with fig trees growing out of them, and the ruined stretches are the ones worth walking.
season: Apr–May and Oct — high summer means no shade and hard light on the brick
tip: Walk the stretch from Silivrikapı north to Edirnekapı in the morning and stay outside the wall on the moat side; the inside is a building site of car repair yards.
todo: Belgrat Kapı and its restored towers
The bostan market gardens in the moat
Mermerkule ruins on the Marmara shore
rev: Those who walk a full section find it the most atmospheric thing in the city; everyone warns that some stretches are unlit, dogs roam the moat, restoration quality is patchy and it is best not done alone after dark.
entry: Free
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M1 metro to Topkapı-Ulubatlı or the T4 tram to Edirnekapı; walk the wall in one direction and take a bus back

name: Chora Church (Kariye Mosque)
desc: The finest late-Byzantine mosaics anywhere, packed into two small narthexes: the life of the Virgin, the Journey to Bethlehem, faces with real weight and modelling. The side chapel holds the Anastasis fresco, Christ hauling Adam and Eve out of their tombs by the wrists. It reopened as a working mosque in 2024 after long restoration.
season: Year-round — closed Wednesdays in some seasons; check before travelling out
tip: The mosaic narthexes stay visible but the nave is now carpeted and screened, so go mid-morning on a weekday and give the Anastasis chapel at the south end the time it deserves.
todo: Anastasis fresco in the parekklesion
Journey to Bethlehem mosaic
Dome of the Virgin's ancestors
rev: The mosaics are almost universally called the best in the city, but visitors report confusion over the post-2024 mosque arrangement, curtains covering part of the nave, restricted hours around prayers and a long ride out to Edirnekapı for a small building.
entry: ≈€20 for foreign visitors · arrangements changed with the 2024 reopening, check on the day
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M2 to Vezneciler and bus 87, or the T4 tram to Edirnekapı and a 10-min walk downhill

name: Yedikule Fortress
desc: Mehmed II bolted a five-towered Ottoman keep onto the Golden Gate of the Theodosian walls, creating a courtyard treasury and later a prison where an eighteen-year-old sultan was strangled. The marble Golden Gate, once faced in gold, is bricked up but still there. Reopened after restoration with walkways along the ramparts.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the courtyard is bare and hot in midsummer
tip: Walk out of the north gate afterwards to the Yedikule bostans, the walled market gardens that have grown lettuce in the same soil since Byzantine times.
todo: The bricked-up Golden Gate
Prison graffiti in the inscription tower
Rampart walk over the market gardens
rev: Visitors like the emptiness and the rampart views over the Marmara, while noting the restoration has been over-tidy, the labelling is minimal and the surrounding district gives little reason to linger.
entry: Small fee — check locally · usually covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then Marmaray suburban rail to Kazlıçeşme and a 10-min walk, or the T1 tram to Zeytinburnu and a short taxi

name: Rüstem Pasha Mosque
desc: Hidden above the hardware shops of the Eminönü bazaar streets and reached by an unmarked stair, this small Sinan mosque carries the densest İznik tilework in Istanbul — tomato-red tulips and carnations covering the piers, the mihrab wall and even the outer porch. The 2021 restoration brought the reds back to full strength.
season: Year-round; late morning light on the porch tiles is best
tip: The entrance is a dark doorway between shops on Hasırcılar Caddesi with a small brass plate — look for the stair, not for a courtyard.
todo: Tiled outer porch under the eaves
Tulip panels on the four piers
The stair entrance off Hasırcılar Caddesi
rev: Repeatedly called the best tiles in Turkey outside a museum, with the usual caveats: hard to find, tiny inside, closed at prayer times and increasingly full of photographers since it reopened.
entry: Free
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then metro and T1 tram to Eminönü; it is three minutes uphill behind the Spice Bazaar

name: Eyüp Sultan Mosque
desc: The holiest Ottoman site in the city, built over the grave of the Prophet's standard-bearer who died besieging Constantinople. The courtyard has plane trees, storks of pilgrims in white, and boys in sequinned circumcision costume being photographed. The tomb chamber opposite is lined in İznik blue and the queue to it never really stops.
season: Year-round; Ramadan evenings are extraordinary but jammed
tip: Come on a weekday morning rather than a Friday, and buy a paper cone of pilgrim sweets from the stalls on the approach — the boiled candy shops here are the original ones.
todo: Tomb chamber's İznik panels
The ancient plane tree in the courtyard
Ottoman tombs lining the approach street
rev: Visitors call the atmosphere the most genuinely religious in Istanbul and worth the trip up the Horn, while noting the crush at the tomb, strict dress enforcement and a commercial approach street thick with stalls.
entry: Free · conservative dress expected, this is a pilgrimage site
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M7 metro to Eyüpsultan, or the Golden Horn ferry from Eminönü straight to Eyüp pier

name: Pierre Loti Hill
desc: A café terrace at the top of the Eyüp cemetery, looking straight down the Golden Horn with the water bending away towards Galata. The walk up through the graveyard is the real attraction: cypresses, turbaned Ottoman headstones tilting at all angles, cats, and almost total silence a few minutes above a busy shrine.
season: Sep–Nov for clear air; hazy and hot Jul–Aug, muddy Jan–Feb
tip: Walk up through the cemetery and take the cable car down, not the other way round — and skip the terrace café, which trades on the view.
todo: Ottoman headstones on the cemetery path
Sunset over the Golden Horn
Cable car down to Eyüp pier
rev: The view earns the trip and the cemetery walk surprises people, but the café is widely called overpriced and mediocre, the terrace is packed at weekends and the cable car queue can run past thirty minutes.
entry: Free · cable car a few lira each way
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M7 metro to Eyüpsultan, or the Golden Horn ferry from Eminönü to Eyüp and the TF2 cable car

name: The Golden Horn
desc: A seven-kilometre drowned valley cutting into the European side, once the imperial harbour, then an industrial sewer, now cleaned enough that cormorants fish it. Small ferries thread from Eminönü up to Eyüp past shipyards, the iron Bulgarian church, and the wooden houses of Balat, with the Süleymaniye on the ridge above.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — winter southerlies make the small ferries choppy
tip: Take the Haliç ferry line rather than a tour boat: it costs a couple of lira with an İstanbulkart, stops where you actually want to get off, and locals use it.
todo: Haliç ferry Eminönü to Eyüp
Fishermen on the Galata Bridge lower deck
Rahmi Koç Museum at Hasköy
rev: People rate the cheap ferry as the best value in the city, though the water still smells in still August weather, the shoreline path is broken by roads, and the Hasköy and Kasımpaşa banks remain scruffy.
entry: Free · ferry fare a few lira with an İstanbulkart
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then metro to Haliç or Eminönü; the Haliç ferry line runs roughly hourly from Eminönü

name: Grand Bazaar
desc: Sixty-one covered streets and around four thousand shops under painted vaults, laid out by trade since the fifteenth century. The tourist arteries sell the same lamps and evil eyes; two turns off them you find the gold casters, the bead sellers, and the İç Bedesten, the oldest stone core, where antique dealers work.
season: Year-round · closed Sundays and public holidays
tip: Go in through the Nuruosmaniye gate and head straight to the İç Bedesten, then out to the Sahaflar book market by the Beyazıt gate — that route skips most of the hustle.
todo: İç Bedesten antique core
Zincirli Han courtyard for carpets
Şark Kahvesi for a break
rev: Most enjoy an hour of it and find the architecture better than the goods; the persistent complaints are aggressive touting, tourist pricing on everything from carpets to tea, and getting lost with no useful signage.
entry: Free · closed Sundays
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then metro and the T1 tram to Beyazıt-Kapalıçarşı or Çemberlitaş, both gates a minute away

name: Spice Bazaar and Eminönü
desc: An L-shaped seventeenth-century hall that smells of cumin and dried rose, built to fund the New Mosque next door. The real market is outside it: the streets behind sell cheese, olives, coffee roasted at Kurukahveci Mehmet Efendi, live pigeons and fishing tackle, and prices there are half what they are inside.
season: Year-round; mornings before eleven for the food streets
tip: Buy your saffron and pistachios in the outer streets, not the covered hall, and queue at Mehmet Efendi on the corner for coffee ground while you wait.
todo: Coffee queue at Kurukahveci Mehmet Efendi
Cheese and pastırma on Hasırcılar Caddesi
Balık ekmek boats at the pier
rev: Loved for the smell and the food streets around it, criticised for hard-sell inside the hall, inflated prices on saffron and Turkish delight, and a crush at the doors that makes pickpocketing a genuine risk.
entry: Free
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then metro and the T1 tram to Eminönü, or any Bosphorus ferry to Eminönü pier

name: Karaköy
desc: The old Genoese port quarter under Galata, now the best eating in the city: chandlers and ship-fitters on one street, third-wave coffee and mezes on the next. Karaköy Güllüoğlu still cuts baklava behind glass at the ferry end, and the fish restaurants under the bridge grill hamsi in winter.
season: Year-round; May–Jun and Sep–Oct for outdoor tables
tip: Eat pistachio baklava standing at Güllüoğlu's counter, then take the Tünel — the 1875 funicular, second-oldest underground railway in the world — up to Beyoğlu instead of walking the hill.
todo: Baklava at Karaköy Güllüoğlu
Tünel funicular up to İstiklal
Kılıç Ali Paşa mosque and hamam
rev: Widely called the best place to eat in Istanbul, though regulars complain gentrification has pushed prices to European levels, the waterfront is a permanent construction site and the cruise terminal has changed the mood.
entry: Free
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M11+M2 to Şişhane and downhill, or any ferry to Karaköy pier; the T1 tram stops on the bridge

name: Kadıköy
desc: The Asian side's centre and where Istanbul actually eats and drinks. The fish market grid around Güneşlibahçe Sokak has pickle shops, pastırma counters and a hundred meyhane tables; Moda a few streets on is bookshops, tea gardens on the seawall and a coast path where the whole neighbourhood walks at dusk.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — Moda's seafront is bleak in a February northerly
tip: Cross by the Eminönü–Kadıköy ferry rather than the Marmaray tunnel, sit on the right for the Topkapı profile, and eat at the market before eight when it fills.
todo: Çiya Sofrası on Güneşlibahçe Sokak
Pickle juice at a turşucu
Moda seawall walk at sunset
rev: Repeat visitors say this is where they would live, but note that the market streets are shoulder-to-shoulder on weekend evenings, prices have climbed steeply, and the bar zone gets loud until very late.
entry: Free
onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then the M4 metro straight to Kadıköy; from the European side take the ferry from Eminönü or Karaköy

name: Balat
desc: The old Jewish quarter on the Golden Horn, a grid of steep lanes with painted timber houses, the Ahrida Synagogue with its boat-shaped bimah, and old-iron shops that have become antique cafés. Kiremit Caddesi and Vodina Caddesi carry the colour; one street back it is still laundry lines and men playing okey.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; Sunday mornings are quietest
tip: The synagogues need advance permission through the Chief Rabbinate, so arrange that days ahead — turning up at the door will not get you in.
todo: Coloured houses on Kiremit Caddesi
Ahrida Synagogue by appointment
Forno or a bakery breakfast on Vodina
rev: Charming and photogenic by consensus, but locals and visitors alike now complain about influencer queues at the painted-stair corner, café prices out of step with the neighbourhood, and residents tired of cameras.
entry: Free · synagogue visits by prior arrangement only
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then metro to Haliç and bus, or the Golden Horn ferry from Eminönü to Ayvansaray/Balat pier

name: Fener
desc: Balat's Greek neighbour, dominated by the red-brick Phanar Greek College standing on the hill like a Victorian asylum. Below it, the Ecumenical Patriarchate keeps a courtyard, a modest cathedral and a gate welded shut since a patriarch was hanged from it in 1821. Steep cobbled lanes, a few surviving Greek families, and cats everywhere.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the lanes are treacherous in winter rain
tip: Inside the Patriarchate church, look for the column of the flagellation and the mosaic-covered patriarchal throne — and note the sealed Orta Kapı as you leave.
todo: St George's cathedral at the Patriarchate
Phanar Greek College from the hill
Church of St Mary of the Mongols
rev: Visitors find the Patriarchate quietly moving and the hill walk rewarding, while complaining that the Greek College cannot be entered, the streets are steep and poorly lit, and several churches keep unpredictable hours.
entry: Free · Patriarchate open most mornings, modest dress
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then metro to Haliç and a short bus, or the Golden Horn ferry from Eminönü to Fener pier

name: Samatya
desc: A Marmara-shore quarter of Armenian and Greek descent that tourists almost never reach, built around a square of meyhanes where the meze trolley still comes to the table and the rakı is cheap. Surp Kevork church anchors one side; behind it, low houses, a Sunday fish market, and the Byzantine Studios monastery ruin ten minutes west.
season: Year-round; Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct for square tables outdoors
tip: Come on a Friday or Saturday evening when the meyhane square fills and a fasıl band works the tables — midweek it is half asleep.
todo: Meyhane dinner on the square
Surp Kevork Armenian church
Studios monastery ruin at İmrahor
rev: Those who find it call it the last unposed neighbourhood on the peninsula, though the meyhanes are hit and miss, English is rare and the Studios ruin is often locked behind its fence.
entry: Free
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then Marmaray suburban rail to Kocamustafapaşa, which is a five-minute walk from the square

name: Bulgarian St Stephen Church
desc: A neo-Gothic church cast entirely in iron in Vienna in 1893, shipped down the Danube and Black Sea in sections and bolted together on the Golden Horn shore. Every pilaster, gallery and rosette is metal, painted to look like stone. Restored in 2018, it now gleams cream and gold in a small waterside garden.
season: Year-round; morning light comes off the water onto the façade
tip: Rap on the caretaker's door if the church looks shut — it usually opens on request outside services, and the ironwork detail only reads from inside the galleries.
todo: Cast-iron gallery brackets inside
Riverside garden and Bulgarian graves
Compare panels with the painted 'stone'
rev: People are consistently surprised by how convincing the fake stone is and how empty the place is, though the interior is small, opening hours are erratic and the traffic on the shore road spoils the setting.
entry: Free · donation box inside
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then metro to Haliç and a bus along the shore, or the Golden Horn ferry to Fener pier and a two-minute walk

name: Dolmabahçe Palace
desc: Six hundred metres of white marble along the Bosphorus, built in the 1850s when the empire could not afford it. The ceremonial hall carries a four-and-a-half-tonne Bohemian chandelier under a thirty-six-metre dome, and there is a crystal staircase with banisters of Baccarat glass. Atatürk died here; every clock reads 09:05.
season: Year-round · closed Mondays; the seaside garden is best in May
tip: Tickets are timed and the palace often sells out by noon in summer — book online, and take the Harem supplement only if you have two hours, since the tour is walked at a set pace.
todo: Crystal staircase of Baccarat glass
Ceremonial hall chandelier
Atatürk's room with the stopped clock
rev: Impressive to almost everyone and gaudy to some, with steady complaints about compulsory guided groups moved along briskly, no photography inside, long queues at the gate and a price that does not include the Harem.
entry: ≈€40 combined Selamlık and Harem · National Palaces ticket, not on the Museum Pass · closed Mondays
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M11+M2 to Şişhane and the T1 tram to Kabataş, a five-minute walk along the shore

name: Beylerbeyi Palace
desc: The sultans' summer place on the Asian shore, directly under the first Bosphorus bridge, with a marble pool and fountain inside the entrance hall to cool the air. Empress Eugénie stayed and copied its windows for the Tuileries. Outside, two seaside kiosks and a terrace where the current runs fast and green past the wall.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct · closed Mondays
tip: Combine it with a walk south along the shore into Beylerbeyi village for tea by the mosque; the ferry pier there is a working local one, not a tourist stop.
todo: Indoor marble pool in the entrance hall
Sea kiosks on the terrace
Tea by the village mosque afterwards
rev: Far quieter than Dolmabahçe and rated better value, though visits are guided and brisk, photography is restricted, and the bridge roaring overhead is louder than the photographs prepare you for.
entry: ≈€15 · National Palaces ticket, not on the Museum Pass · closed Mondays
onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then M4 to Üsküdar and bus 15 along the shore, or a ferry to Üsküdar and a 10-min taxi

name: Küçüksu Pavilion
desc: A small rococo hunting lodge on the Asian shore between two streams, all curls and shells in white marble, with a double staircase running down to a landing stage on the water. Two rooms up, two down — it was built for afternoons, not for living. The meadow behind it was the Ottoman picnic ground called the Sweet Waters of Asia.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct · closed Mondays
tip: Walk five minutes north to the Küçüksu fountain of Mihrişah Sultan and then on to Anadoluhisarı — the whole shore stretch takes half an hour and hardly anyone does it.
todo: Marble staircase down to the water
Parquet floors and painted ceilings
Walk on to Anadoluhisarı
rev: Visitors like the scale and the emptiness and call it a good hour, but note it is genuinely small for the ticket, awkward to reach without a car, and the garden is fenced off from the shore road.
entry: ≈€8 · National Palaces ticket, not on the Museum Pass · closed Mondays
onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then M4 to Üsküdar and bus 15 up the Asian shore; by car, park at Anadoluhisarı and walk

name: The Bosphorus Ferry
desc: The city's best sightseeing is a commuter boat. The full Şehir Hatları run goes from Eminönü to Anadolu Kavağı in about ninety minutes, past Dolmabahçe, the two fortresses, wooden yalı mansions on both banks and under three bridges, with tea sold from a tray and gulls taking simit out of passengers' hands.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct; winter crossings are cold and wet on deck but half empty
tip: Take the long tour outbound and come back on the short hop or a bus, or you lose three hours; sit on the right going up for the European yalıs.
todo: Sit on the open upper deck with tea
Yalı mansions between Kandilli and Kanlıca
Lunch stop at Anadolu Kavağı
rev: Almost everyone rates it the best value in Istanbul, with complaints about deck seats gone twenty minutes before departure, a rushed and touristy lunch stop at the top, and private tour boats overselling the same route.
entry: ≈€8 for the full Şehir Hatları round trip · short hops a few lira with an İstanbulkart
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then metro and T1 tram to Eminönü; the long Bosphorus boat leaves from the Boğaz İskelesi pier

name: Arnavutköy
desc: A row of nineteenth-century timber houses standing directly in the water on the European shore, bay windows overhanging the current. Behind them a couple of steep streets, an Ottoman-Greek church, and fish restaurants on the Akıntı Burnu point where the Bosphorus runs hardest. Bebek's expensive cafés are a fifteen-minute walk south.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct; the point is windswept from November
tip: Walk the shore path from Bebek to Arnavutköy at dusk and eat at one of the small back-street fish places rather than the waterfront ones charging for the view.
todo: Timber yalı row from the water side
Fish dinner at Akıntı Burnu
Strawberry sellers in the back lanes
rev: Consistently called the prettiest street of wooden houses left on the Bosphorus, with the caveats that the coast road runs right behind them, parking is impossible and the waterfront restaurants are priced for Bebek.
entry: Free
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M11+M2 to Levent and bus down to the shore, or the T1 tram to Kabataş and bus 22/25E along the Bosphorus

name: Kuzguncuk
desc: One street, İcadiye Caddesi, running up a valley from the Bosphorus, lined with painted wooden houses in ochre, lilac and green. A mosque and a synagogue stand on the same corner and a Greek and an Armenian church a hundred metres apart. Halfway up there is a market garden that residents fought developers to keep.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — spring wisteria on the house fronts
tip: Come on a weekday morning; on Sunday the one street is a slow parade of photo shoots and the breakfast places have hour-long waits.
todo: Painted houses on İcadiye Caddesi
The bostan market garden
Mosque and synagogue on one corner
rev: Charming and genuinely lived-in by most accounts, though weekend crowds, café prices well above the Asian-side average and residents' visible irritation at cameras come up again and again.
entry: Free
onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then M4 to Üsküdar and bus 15 north, or a ferry to Üsküdar and a 20-min walk along the shore

name: Çengelköy
desc: An Asian-shore village known for its small ridged cucumbers and for the plane tree at Çınaraltı, under which the tea garden has served the same glass of tea for a century. The shore has yalıs, a naval school, and a promenade where families walk with the Bosphorus current a metre away. Beylerbeyi is the next stop south.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct; the tea garden works year-round with braziers
tip: Order a Turkish breakfast at Çınaraltı and ask for the local cucumbers with it, then walk the shore north towards Kuleli for the best view of the Rumeli side.
todo: Breakfast under the plane tree at Çınaraltı
Kuleli military school from the shore
Buy Çengelköy cucumbers at a greengrocer
rev: Locals rate the breakfast and the shore walk highly; visitors report weekend queues at Çınaraltı, patchy service, and a coast road that carries a lot of traffic behind the promenade.
entry: Free
onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then M4 to Üsküdar and bus 15, or the Beşiktaş–Çengelköy ferry which is the pleasant way in

name: Rumeli Hisarı
desc: Mehmed II built this fortress in four months in 1452 at the narrowest point of the strait to cut Constantinople off from the Black Sea. Three huge towers and a curtain wall run straight up a steep slope, so the walk inside is all steps. Below it, a village of fish restaurants and a cemetery of Ottoman headstones.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the slope inside is punishing in July heat
tip: Climb the north tower for the shot straight down the Bosphorus at the Fatih bridge, then eat waffles or fish in the village below rather than inside the tourist strip.
todo: North tower view at the narrows
Cannon collection in the courtyard
Fish lunch in the village below
rev: The views are almost universally praised, but the site is steep with uneven steps and no railings in places, parts are periodically closed for restoration, and there is little shade or interpretation inside.
entry: ≈€10 · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye · closed Wednesdays in some seasons
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M11+M2 to Levent and bus, or bus 25E/22 up the Bosphorus shore road from Kabataş

name: Anadolu Hisarı
desc: The older, smaller fortress on the Asian bank, thrown up by Bayezid I in the 1390s and now half-swallowed by a village of wooden houses at the mouth of the Göksu stream. You cannot go in, but the walls run straight through the neighbourhood with washing lines beside them and rowing boats tied under the keep.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the stream mouth is best in morning light
tip: Walk under the Fatih bridge from Küçüksu, then take a rowing boat up the Göksu stream from the little landing — it is the old Sweet Waters excursion and costs almost nothing.
todo: Keep walls from the Göksu bridge
Rowing boat up the Göksu
Wooden yalıs along the shore road
rev: People like stumbling on a fourteenth-century castle inside a working village, though the fortress interior has been closed for years, there is no signage, and traffic on the shore road makes photographing it awkward.
entry: Free · fortress interior closed, viewed from outside
onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then M4 to Üsküdar and bus 15 north, or the Kandilli ferry and a 20-minute shore walk

name: Anadolu Kavağı and Yoros Castle
desc: The last village before the Black Sea, and the turnaround point of the long Bosphorus ferry. A twenty-minute climb above it stands Yoros, a Byzantine castle on the headland where the strait opens out, with two ruined towers and a marble gate. From the top you see the Black Sea on one side and the whole strait on the other.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct; fog and wind off the Black Sea from November
tip: The ferry gives you about three hours ashore — climb to Yoros first and eat afterwards, because the fish restaurants by the pier fill the moment the boat docks.
todo: Climb to Yoros Castle gate
Black Sea view from the headland
Fried mussels at the pier
rev: The castle walk is rated the best part of the Bosphorus trip, while the village itself draws complaints about aggressive restaurant touts, tourist pricing on fish and a scramble back to the boat at departure time.
entry: Free · the castle is open ground with no gate or ticket
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then metro and tram to Eminönü for the long Bosphorus ferry; by land, bus 15A from Üsküdar via Beykoz

name: Büyükada
desc: The largest of the Princes' Islands, an hour and a half out into the Marmara: no private cars, pine woods, and streets of enormous timber mansions with fretwork verandas built by Greek and Armenian merchants. Two hills, each with a monastery — St George's on the southern one, reached by a path where pilgrims tie rags of cloth to the trees.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — July and August are packed; many places shut Nov–Mar
tip: Rent a bicycle or take an electric shuttle to the Lunapark saddle, then walk the last steep kilometre to Aya Yorgi; the phaeton horses were retired in 2020 and the replacements are limited.
todo: Aya Yorgi monastery on the south hill
Timber mansions on Çankaya Caddesi
Swim at Yörükali or Nizam beach
rev: The car-free quiet and the mansions win people over, but summer weekends bring ferry queues in both directions, beach clubs charging a full day rate for a sunbed, and a very crowded main street near the pier.
entry: Free · ferry from Kabataş or Bostancı, a few lira with an İstanbulkart
onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then M4 to Bostancı and the island ferry; from Europe, ferries leave Kabataş and Eminönü

name: Heybeliada
desc: The second island, greener and calmer than Büyükada, with a naval school on the waterfront and the Halki Greek Orthodox seminary on the north hill, closed since 1971 but visitable in its grounds. A circular road runs round the pine-covered edge; the coves on the far side are quiet enough to swim off the rocks.
season: Jun–Sep for swimming, May and Oct for walking the ring road
tip: Walk or cycle the ring road anticlockwise and stop at Değirmen Burnu on the west side, where there is shade, a small beach and none of the pier crowd.
todo: Halki seminary grounds on the hill
Ring road walk to Değirmen Burnu
Swim off the rocks at Çam Limanı
rev: Regulars prefer it to Büyükada for the quiet and the pines, though the seminary building itself cannot be entered, restaurants near the pier are ordinary and ferries thin out badly out of season.
entry: Free · ferry from Kabataş or Bostancı, a few lira with an İstanbulkart
onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then M4 to Bostancı and the island ferry, which calls at Heybeliada before Büyükada

name: Burgazada
desc: The small island with the strongest Greek residue and the smallest crowd: one hill, one loop road, a domed church at the top and the house of the writer Sait Faik kept exactly as he left it in 1954, down to his fishing tackle. Kalpazankaya on the far shore is a rock cove with a fish restaurant on the terrace above it.
season: Jun–Sep to swim; May and Oct for the loop walk without heat
tip: Walk the ninety minutes round to Kalpazankaya for a late lunch and the sunset over the Marmara, then take the last ferry back rather than the crowded afternoon boats.
todo: Sait Faik Museum in his old house
Aya Yani church at the top
Swim at Kalpazankaya rocks
rev: Visitors call it the island to choose if you want quiet, with the trade-offs that there is almost nothing to do beyond walking and swimming, few places to eat, and ferry connections are sparser than to the bigger islands.
entry: Free · museum free · ferry a few lira with an İstanbulkart
onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then M4 to Bostancı and the island ferry; Burgazada is the second stop from the mainland

name: Kınalıada
desc: The nearest island, forty minutes out, red-earthed and almost treeless where the others are pine — the name means henna island, from the iron in the rock. Largely Armenian in population, with a modern church shaped like a wedge and a shoreline of flat rocks that locals swim from all summer. Byzantine emperors were exiled here.
season: Jun–Sep for swimming; bare and windswept the rest of the year
tip: It is the fastest island escape from the city for a swim after work — the rock platforms on the western shore beyond the mosque are free, unlike the beach clubs by the pier.
todo: Swim off the western rock shelves
Armenian church of Surp Krikor Lusavoriç
Walk up Çınar hill for the Marmara view
rev: Praised as the quickest way out of Istanbul into the sea, but honestly reported as the plainest island: little shade, no forest, limited food, and beach clubs that charge disproportionately for a sunbed.
entry: Free · ferry a few lira with an İstanbulkart · beach clubs charge separately
onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then M4 to Bostancı and the island ferry; from Europe the Kabataş boat reaches it first

name: Karacaahmet Cemetery
desc: One of the largest Islamic burial grounds in the world, seven hundred years old and covering more than seven hundred acres of Üsküdar under black cypresses. The older sections have marble headstones carved with turbans that indicate the dead man's rank, and women's stones cut with flowers. Traffic noise disappears fifty metres in.
season: Year-round; Oct–Nov light through the cypresses is the best of it
tip: Enter from the Nuh Kuyusu gate on the south side and head for the oldest section near the Miskinler tekke, where the turbaned stones stand thickest.
todo: Turbaned Ottoman headstones
Şakirin Mosque at the north edge
Cypress avenues in low autumn light
rev: Those who go find it silent and extraordinary, though there are no maps or paths marked, funerals are frequent and visitors are asked to be discreet, and much of the modern part is ordinary municipal cemetery.
entry: Free · a working cemetery, dress and behave accordingly
onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then M4 to Üsküdar; the cemetery starts a 10-minute walk inland from the ferry pier

name: Çamlıca Hill
desc: At 268 metres the highest point in the city, a pine-topped hill on the Asian side with the entire Bosphorus laid out beneath it — three bridges, the Golden Horn, the old peninsula's domes, and the Marmara with the islands beyond. An Ottoman-style tea garden sits under the pines; the vast new mosque occupies the next summit south.
season: Sep–Nov and Mar–May for clear air; summer haze flattens the view
tip: Go two hours before sunset on a day after rain, when the air is washed clean and you can see the islands — and use the Küçük Çamlıca hill next door if the main terrace is full.
todo: Tea in the terrace garden at sunset
Spot all three Bosphorus bridges
Çamlıca Mosque courtyard next door
rev: The panorama is agreed to be the best in the city, but the hill is often hazy, the tea garden gets very crowded at weekends, the TV masts intrude on photographs and there is no public transport to the summit.
entry: Free · small parking charge
onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then M5 metro to Bulgurlu and a 15-min uphill walk or short taxi; by car, park below the tea garden

name: Şile
desc: Istanbul's own Black Sea town, seventy kilometres from Üsküdar over forest roads: a white and black striped lighthouse on the cliff, a Genoese castle on an offshore rock, and long sand beaches with real surf. The cotton cloth called şile bezi is woven here and sold from shops around the square, cheaply and without much ceremony.
season: Jun–Sep for the sea; the town half closes Nov–Mar and the wind is bitter
tip: The rip currents off the town beaches are genuinely dangerous — swim only where the flags and lifeguards are, and use Ayazma or Kumbaba rather than the unpatrolled coves.
todo: Şile lighthouse on the headland
Genoese castle rock at sunset
Buy şile bezi cloth in the square
rev: Locals rate the beaches and the fish, but every account mentions dangerous currents and drownings each summer, weekend traffic out of the city, and a town centre that is more concrete than picturesque.
entry: Free · beach clubs charge for sunbeds
onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then bus 139 from Üsküdar via Şile road, about 90 minutes; a car is far easier and the forest road is good

name: Ağva
desc: A village on the Black Sea coast where two rivers, the Göksu and the Yeşilçay, come down through forest to the same beach. Small hotels line the riverbanks with jetties and rowing boats, and the whole point is doing nothing for two days: river breakfast, a boat upstream under overhanging trees, grilled fish, sleep.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — August weekends are booked out, winter is wet and shut
tip: Take a boat up the Yeşilçay rather than the Göksu, and book a riverside room midweek; on Saturdays the two-hour drive from Istanbul can double.
todo: Rowing boat up the Yeşilçay
Breakfast on a river jetty
Walk to Kilimli Bay cove
rev: Couples call it the easiest escape from the city and the river setting genuinely lovely, while complaining about heavy weekend traffic, hotel prices that spike in July and August, and a beach with the same Black Sea currents as Şile.
entry: Free · boat trips priced per hour, agree the fare first
onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then bus 139 to Şile and a connecting minibus, roughly two hours; most people drive

name: Kilyos
desc: The European side's Black Sea beach, thirty-five kilometres north of the city past Sarıyer: a broad arc of grey-gold sand with real waves, backed by dunes and beach clubs that run day beds, music and volleyball through the summer. A Genoese tower stands on the hill behind and the water is noticeably colder than the Marmara.
season: Jun–early Sep only; out of season the clubs shut and the wind is raw
tip: The undertow here kills people every summer — stay between the flags at a lifeguarded club, and go on a weekday because Saturday turns the road from Sarıyer into a car park.
todo: Swim between the flags at a patrolled club
Genoese tower on the hill
Walk north along the dunes
rev: Convenient and genuinely sandy for a city beach, but reviews are consistent about strong rip currents, club entry fees that feel steep for what you get, loud music, and litter after busy weekends.
entry: Beach club day entry roughly ₺500–1500 (≈€11–33) depending on the club and the day
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M11 to Hacıosman and bus 151 from Sarıyer, about 40 minutes; parking at the clubs in summer is difficult

name: Riva
desc: A river mouth on the Asian Black Sea coast with a ruined Genoese castle on the bluff, a long empty beach and a handful of fish shacks where the Riva stream meets the sea. It is thirty minutes from Beykoz and most Istanbullus have still never been; the football federation's training camp is its only landmark.
season: Jun–Sep for the beach; the castle walk is best in Apr–May
tip: Park at the village and walk north over the bluff to the castle ruin, then eat at one of the river-mouth places where the fish comes from the boats tied outside.
todo: Genoese castle ruin on the headland
Fish lunch at the river mouth
Long walk on the empty sand
rev: Those who go like the emptiness and the cheap fish, but note the same Black Sea rip currents with no lifeguards, a scruffy village centre, and construction creeping along the coast road from Beykoz.
entry: Free
onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then M5 to Üsküdar and bus 15 to Beykoz, then a local minibus; a car makes it a 45-minute run

name: Belgrad Forest
desc: Five thousand hectares of oak and beech north of the city that supplied Istanbul's water for four centuries, still holding Ottoman reservoirs, dams and stone aqueducts among the trees. Neşetsuyu and Bentler have marked trails and running loops; on autumn mornings mist sits between the trunks and the city is completely gone.
season: Apr–Jun for green and Oct–Nov for colour; winter is muddy but atmospheric
tip: Enter at Neşetsuyu on a weekday for the quiet trails; the Bentler entrance on a Sunday is a mangal picnic ground with smoke and speakers, not a forest walk.
todo: Sultan Mahmud dam and reservoir
Neşetsuyu running loop
Atatürk Arboretum in Bahçeköy
rev: Istanbullus treat it as the city's lung and praise the trails, while complaining about weekend barbecue crowds, litter around the picnic areas, and entrance fees per person and per car that have risen sharply.
entry: Small entrance fee per person and per car — check locally · Arboretum ticketed separately
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M11 to Hacıosman and bus 42 to Bahçeköy; a car is much easier for reaching the far entrances

name: Mağlova Aqueduct
desc: Sinan's finest piece of engineering, a two-tier limestone aqueduct 257 metres long striding across the Alibey valley north of the city, built in the 1560s to carry Belgrad Forest water to Istanbul. It stands almost alone in scrubland above a reservoir, with buttresses shaped like ships' prows to split the current when the valley floods.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the track in is impassable mud after heavy rain
tip: The final approach is an unsurfaced track off the Cebeci road and there is no sign — set the coordinates before you leave, and do not attempt it in a low car after rain.
todo: Walk under the lower arches
Prow-shaped buttresses at the piers
Uzunkemer aqueduct nearby on the same system
rev: Those who find it call it the most impressive Ottoman structure nobody visits; the complaints are all about access — no public transport, an unmarked dirt track, rubbish dumped at the approach and rising reservoir water at times.
entry: Free · open land, no gate
onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then a hire car; it is roughly 25 km north-west of the centre via Cebeci, with the last 2 km on a rough track

name: Polonezköy
desc: A Polish village founded in 1842 by exiles granted land by the sultan, sitting in forest above Beykoz with a Catholic church, a Polish cemetery and a few families still carrying Polish surnames. It survives on Sunday lunch: pork — rare in Turkey — smoked sausage, pancakes and mulberry trees you can eat straight from in June.
season: May–Jun for mulberries, Oct–Nov for the forest colour; midweek always quieter
tip: Book a table before you drive out on a Sunday, and walk the marked forest paths in the nature park behind the village rather than just eating and leaving.
todo: Sunday lunch with Polish sausage
Zofia Ryży house and village museum
Forest trails in the nature park
rev: People enjoy the oddity and the food, but say the Polish character is now thin, restaurants are overpriced for what arrives, and weekend traffic on the narrow forest road out of Beykoz is grim.
entry: Free · nature park charges a small entry per car
onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then M5 to Üsküdar and bus to Beykoz plus a minibus; realistically it is a 45-minute drive from the Asian side
